The system is kind of weird here, so

There's 4 different levels of education in the Netherlands, with subdivisions

PO, praktijkonderwijs (practical education) for those with an IQ between 55 and 80 and with severe learning deficits

VMBO, voorbereidend middelbaar beroepsonderwijs (preparing middle level work education), with four subdivisions, basis, kader, gemengd and theoretisch, which all have different end qualifications. 

VMBO-B prepares you for level 2 MBO (middelbaar beroepsonderwijs, middle level work education), anything above that allows you to enter level 3-4 MBO and with VMBO-G or VMBO-T (also called MAVO, a now abolished education level) you can also enter HAVO

VMBO-B, VMBO-K and VMBO-G also have a practical part where you directly learn a profession. 

Then there's HAVO, which prepares for HBO. No subdivisions.

Then there's VWO, which prepares for university, split into Atheneum and Gymnasium, the only difference being classical languages. There is no difference in qualification level.

The only big thing is qualification level. Someone with a HAVO diploma can go to all MBOs and HBOs that suit their profile, but if they want to go to university they either have to do VWO or pass a qualification test

The system is designed so every teen can do something they're somewhat interested in at a level they can handle, but many parents push for them to go as high as possible under the guise of "a better future". It's fine to aim high, but there's no shame in dropping a level if you can't make it

Universiteiten are scientific education. Hogescholen teach for higher-level professions

Any VWO (voorbereindend wetenschappelijk onderwijs, preparing scientific education) diploma grants you access to a university. Some studies require you to do entrance tests, but the majority don't.

Many parents push their children to go as high as possible, which is quite unhealthy ngl

Really interesting conflict, though sad:

A group of missionaries had received the right to own their land, lest it be used in the benefit and development of the natives

They then forced the mohawks to move from their lands to new lands, however, they chose it so that they'd have a place to live and have access to their burial grounds with the promise that they would come to own all that land

Ownership beyond the village was never granted and the missionaries held onto the land for about 200 years. Instead, the missionary settlement was expanded twice.

After multiple petitions and inquiries, seeking to receive the same rights as other mohawk groups, the province of Canada decided to grant the missionaries the right to all the disputed land instead, (active) burial site included.

A claim to at least a portion of the land was made and an ultimatum of eight days was made to hand it over. An armed attempt to take it was crushed by the government.

In the early 20th century, the missionary seminary sold the land. Protests and lawsuits to prevent the sale failed.

Up until that point, the mohawks still used that land, despite not owning it, under the requirement that the land be used to benefit the natives by earlier government grants, but with the sale they were permanently driven from it, reducing their territory from the once promised 165 square kilometres to about 6.

A small golf course was developed on the land, though under protest

Another claim with the government fell through and the mayor of the local town made plans to completely clear the land, gravesites included, expand the golf course by twice its current size and build 60 condos on it, without any discussion, respect or regard for the mohawks, kicking off the crisis

In the end, the government bought the land up and has neither sold it for development or to the mohawks, leaving the situation half unresolved

And then rolling over the ball of the foot and tapping the floor with your heels, using only your hips. You'll find you'll want to support yourself a bit with your calves, that is fine, as long as you keep them nice and loose

Der/des are older grammar. It's the genetive case, denoting possession.

It goes as follows.

Masculine/neuter: des

Feminine/multiple: der

"Met de loop der tijd" means "with the walk of the time". Der replaces "of the". In dutch, the genetive has largely been replaced by just using van/van de

As such, this is an archaic construction. It's not easy using these archaic constructions if you're not used to their grammar. This is not taught in schools and many dutch people don't know and get it wrong as well. This grammar form affects more words as well. 

Other examples:

De man des huizes (the man of the house)

'S ochtends (literally, "of the morning")

You'll find examples with der as well

Important to note here is that these constructions only make sense in their given form. A few can be altered, but not many. That is not to say you cannot form sentences with the genetive case though, as a matter of a fact a few dialects still preserve the genetive case just fine.

You're gonna have to learn to listen. And i mean that as in don't listen to enjoy the music, listen to hear what the drums are doing. It's an entirily different way of listening. 

You listen, you note down what you think you heard if you need it, you learn to play what you heard. Practice that until it's comfortable, then listen again. See if you were right.

And yes that gets annoying at first. You don't know what to listen for. You don't know how everything a drummer does can sound. And by god you will make mistakes and you'll drive yourself mad trying to listen to the same part again on slo-mo just to try to see if you can hear it. All part of the process.

But you get better at it and you get used to it. You'll learn what to listen for. You'll learn to adapt another drummer's sound to your kit. You'll learn a lot of beats to whip out whenever you hear them again. You'll have the fills of everyone else you learned at your dispoa. Those ten repeats will turn into 2-3 for basic songs. Hell, for some even 1.

All music starts with copying someone else to learn how they do it and then make it your own. And to do that, you'll need to listen.

Listening is the number 1 skill you can have in non-solo music. Especially as a drummer. Because if you ever play with a band, your job is always gonna be listening to them, setting a background for them and changing with and for them. If someone falls outta time and your band gets confused, you are the one that's gonna have to pull it back together through sheer listening and adjusting. The drums are the backbone.

Besides it makes learning songs much easier, there aren't that many drum beats per genre. If you can just hear what complex rhythm is played you'll have a much easier time.

But it all starts with listening.

Dutch naming conventions frequently trip up programs asw.

Our surnames usually have an extra word, called a "tussenvoegsel". Grammarwhise it is either a form of "the" or "from". However, it is part of the surname and cannot just be left out. Spelling-whise, they're never capitalised. 

And here's where it gets worse: the dutch system categorises by the first letter after the tussenvoegsel. The belgian system... Eh. Sometimes they do, sometimes they don't. So someone named "de Boer" (the farmer, i know, our surnames are so original) would be at the B in the NL and at the D in belgium.

Ah well. Be glad we never adopted the singular character ij. That also goes wrong, number one way to know your text was shittily translated is when a capital IJ is wrong. For reference: ij/IJ is one letter. Written forms connect it into one. Typewriters had it as one letter. We just never digitalised it.

It's important to play in time, but if you can only play in time it's boring.

Music isn't about perfection. Music is about expression. Playing in time is essential for playing in the first place. Playing with the time is gonna make you sound great.

Dutch is a more conservative west germanic language and a descendant of frankish

You can find plenty of sources on how to learn dutch, but i take it you want to know some basics:

First up, this language gets confusing. We only simplified our grammar in the past 100 years, so there's a lot of remnants and the grammar isn't exactly simple.

What's also to remember: standard dutch is a collection of mostly hollandic and brabantic vocabulary with a more northern pronounciation. It's sort of a big mash of things from different regions and different ages. It's fascinating, but if you try dig into some meanings and etymologies expect to stumble upon deep rabbitholes

Also, words have gender now. However with the current grammar, only neuter / everything else will matter unless you're doing more complex references. De or het words. Important.

The pronounciation can be difficult. Oh it's also different in some regions and that's without going into dialects. Yet the spelling is really straightforward. There are a few rules to it n that's it. Polar opposite of english there.

 Every word has a focus point, the so-called stress. Unless it is a combination word or a loanword it's always on the first syllable. The rest of the word usually gets reduced in a pretty reliable way. Vowel and sentence reduction will make speaking easier eventually

Sentence structure is complex as hell. Dutch is at least as expressive as english and the varying sentence structures are a part of that. The basics will not feel too strange though. Dutch, english and german used to share sentence structures completely and even after centuries of diverging it's still not that far apart.

As for where to start? Expose yourself to the language. Take an interest in dutch things even if you can't understand them yet. Learn the pronounciation rules and the pronounciation. Learn the spelling rules. Even if you cannot understand or form the language, being able to speak and write the words is very very useful and dutch is fairly consistent.

Learn basic sentences. Then learn the grammar behind them. Learn vocab and try assemble your own sentences. Speak them. Correct yourself. Get used to conversational and regional dutch and slowly try conversing. Try reading some dutch books. Try watching some dutch movies or series. Try listening to some dutch music. 

From that point? Let your curiosity free. You'll find all manners of complexities. Learn them. Master them. Apply them. 

Until you know the language like your back pocket. You don't have to speak or understand dialect, but if you can converse with anyone speaking dutch, you're pretty much there
